## Before regex: recall the previous week

If missing income is associated with observed age, the missingness is unlikely to be MCAR. This alone cannot distinguish MAR from MNAR, since income itself could affect whether it is reported. When a cleaning rule changes, keeping raw inputs and the processing version allows us to rerun it and compare outputs.

## The matching question comes first

Use `re.search()` to find a match *within* a string; use `re.fullmatch()` when the entire field must have that format.

```python
import re

zip_pattern = r"\b\d{5}(?:-\d{4})?\b"
examples = ["84043", "84043-4820", "ID84043X", "8404"]

for value in examples:
    found = re.search(zip_pattern, value)
    print(f"{value:12} -> {found.group() if found else None}")
```

```text
84043        -> 84043
84043-4820   -> 84043-4820
ID84043X     -> None
8404         -> None
```

The boundaries prevent a match embedded in letters. If you are checking a dedicated ZIP field, `re.fullmatch()` also rejects surrounding text.

## Whiteboard: four small specifications

Each group takes one problem. Write a pattern on the board, explain why the third example fails, and suggest another test. The example patterns below are **reveals after group explanations**; use the [practice notebook](notebooks/regex_practice.ipynb) first.

| Group | Example whole-field pattern | Should match | Should fail |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| A: ZIP | `\d{5}(?:-\d{4})?` | `84043-4820` | `84043-482` |
| B: phone | `\d{3}[-.]\d{3}[-.]\d{4}` | `801.555.0142` | `8015550142` |
| C: campus email | `[A-Za-z0-9]+@byu\.edu` | `tom7@byu.edu` | `tom@byuXedu` |
| D: citation | `(?:John|Alma) \d+:\d+` | `Alma 34:32` | `Mosiah 3:19` |

For group B, mixed separators also pass. For group C, a dotted username is outside the scope of the initial rule. Both are useful tests when refining a specification.

## Grouping and alternatives

The phone number can use parentheses around its area code or a punctuation mark after it. `(?: ... | ... )` groups those two choices without creating an extraction column.

```python
phone_pattern = r"(?:\(\d{3}\)\s*|\d{3}[-. ])\d{3}[-. ]\d{4}"
numbers = ["801-555-0142", "(801) 555-0142", "801.555.0142"]
print([bool(re.fullmatch(phone_pattern, value)) for value in numbers])
```

```text
[True, True, True]
```

## Email extraction

This classroom pattern finds common addresses. It is an extractor for this task, not a complete validator of all possible email addresses.

```python
email_pattern = r"[\w.+-]+@[\w.-]+\.[A-Za-z]{2,}"
line = "Write first.last+class@byu.edu or help@example.org."
print(re.findall(email_pattern, line))
```

```text
['first.last+class@byu.edu', 'help@example.org']
```

## Read the small talk sample

```python
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd

talks = pd.read_csv(Path("../data/talks_sample.csv"))
print(talks[["talk_name", "conference"]].to_string(index=False))
```

```text
                            talk_name   conference
                      Now Is the Time October 2018
The Sacrament Can Help Us Become Holy October 2016
```

The first talk contains `1\xa0Nephi`, where `\xa0` represents a nonbreaking space. `\s+` matches that space in Python's default Unicode string handling.

**Pause and explain:** Which assumptions in the small group D pattern break for `1 Nephi 8:27`, `D&C 19:16`, and `Alma 34:32–33`?

## Predict a misleading partial match

With a partner, predict what `r"[A-Za-z]+ \d+:\d+"` extracts from `1 Nephi 8:27`, `D&C 19:16`, and `Doctrine and Covenants 121:35`. The actual substrings are `Nephi 8:27`, `C 19:16`, and `Covenants 121:35`. Finding *a* match does not establish that the right information was extracted.

## Construct the citation pattern

The book names below are intentionally limited to names that appear in these two talks. A broader project needs a more complete book list and more tests.

```python
citation_pattern = (
    r"\b(?P<book>Doctrine\s+and\s+Covenants|D&C|[1-3]\s+Nephi|John|Alma|Mosiah)"
    r"\s+(?P<chapter>\d{1,3}):(?P<verse_start>\d{1,3})"
    r"(?:[-–](?P<verse_end>\d{1,3}))?\b"
)

matches = talks["text"].str.extractall(citation_pattern)
citations = matches.reset_index().rename(
    columns={"level_0": "talk_row", "match": "citation_number"}
)
citations.insert(0, "talk_name", talks.loc[citations["talk_row"], "talk_name"].to_numpy())
print(citations[["book", "chapter", "verse_start", "verse_end"]].head(7).to_string(index=False))
```

```text
                  book chapter verse_start verse_end
               1 Nephi       8          27       NaN
               1 Nephi       8          28       NaN
Doctrine and Covenants     121          35       NaN
                  Alma      34          32        33
                  John       8          31        32
                  John      14          17       NaN
                  John      16          33       NaN
```

`extractall()` returns one row per match. A missing `verse_end` means there was no range; it is not a failed extraction. Use `.str.extract()` when you need only the first match per talk.

## Keep the original and normalize the extracted field

```python
citations["book_clean"] = (
    citations["book"]
    .str.replace("\u00a0", " ", regex=False)
    .replace({"D&C": "Doctrine and Covenants"})
)
print(citations.groupby("talk_name").size().to_string())
```

```text
talk_name
Now Is the Time                          7
The Sacrament Can Help Us Become Holy    6
```

The talk text remains untouched. The extracted table can later be joined to talk metadata and compared across processing versions.
